content: The text provided is a long list of references, datasets, and associated publications related to various nutrition and dietary studies conducted across different countries. 1. A baseline survey conducted in 2018 focused on the role of seeds in supporting on-farm biodiversity to promote human health and resilient landscapes. This survey is associated with the publication by Boedecker J, Odhiambo Odour F, Lachat C, Van Damme P, Kennedy G, and Termote C, which highlights how participatory farm diversification and nutrition education improved dietary diversity in Western Kenya. The findings were published in Maternal & Child Nutrition in July 2019 (Volume 15, Issue 3, Article e12803). 2. The ENRICH Project in Kenya, reported by Nutrition International in 2019, conducted formative research to improve nutrition outcomes. The final report, titled ENRICH Kenya Formative Research, was published by Nutrition International in Ottawa. 3. A study by Robert RC, Bartolini RM, Creed-Kanashiro HM, and Verney Sward A utilized formative research to design interventions involving animal-source foods and multiple micronutrient powders. These interventions aimed to enhance micronutrient consumption among infants and young children in Tanzania, Kenya, Bangladesh, and Pakistan. The results were published in Maternal & Child Nutrition in April 2021 (Volume 17, Issue 2, Article e13084). 4. Data from the Malawi iLiNS-DOSE trial, provided by Jaimie Hemsworth, Elaine Ferguson, and Tampere University, were used to analyze nutrient intake. The associated publication by Hemsworth J et al. demonstrated that lipid-based nutrient supplements increased energy and macronutrient intake among Malawian infants. This study was published in the Journal of Nutrition in February 2016 (Volume 146, Issue 2, Pages 326-334). 5. The Malawi Mazira trial data, shared by Bess Caswell and Charles Arnold from the University of California, Davis, examined the impact of egg complementary feeding on energy intake and dietary diversity. The findings were published in Maternal & Child Nutrition in January 2021 (Volume 17, Issue 1, Article e13055). 6. A study in Nigeria, led by De Moura FF et al., investigated cassava intake and vitamin A status among women and preschool children in Akwa-Ibom. The results were published in PLoS One in June 2015 (Volume 10, Issue 6, Article e0129436). 7. The ARCH Project in Senegal, Phase 1, analyzed data on child feeding practices. Alissa Pries and Helen Keller International provided the processed data. The associated publication by Pries AM et al. explored the consumption of commercially produced snack foods and sugar-sweetened beverages during the complementary feeding period in urban contexts across Africa and Asia. This study was published in Maternal & Child Nutrition in October 2017 (Supplement 2, Article e12412). 8. In South Africa, Faber M conducted a study on complementary foods consumed by rural infants aged 6-12 months, revealing inadequate micronutrient content. The findings were published in Public Health Nutrition in June 2005 (Volume 8, Issue 4, Pages 373-381). 9. The ENRICH Project in Tanzania, reported by Nutrition International in 2019, conducted formative research to improve nutrition outcomes. The final report, titled ENRICH Tanzania Formative Research, was published by Nutrition International in Ottawa. 10. Data from Zambia's 2009 Food Consumption and Vitamin A Status Survey were analyzed to assess vitamin A and maize intake among women and children. The associated publication by Hotz C et al. was released in 2011, focusing on nutrition in Central and Eastern Zambia. 11. The Brazilian National Survey on Child Nutrition (ENANI-2019) analyzed dietary data provided by Gilberto Kac and colleagues. The associated publication by Alves-Santos NH et al. detailed the methodological aspects of this population-based household survey, published in Cadernos de Saúde Pública in August 2021 (Volume 37, Issue 8, Article e00300020). 12. The ProPAN four-country study, conducted in Brazil, Jamaica, Mexico, and Panama, aimed to prevent early childhood malnutrition by improving complementary feeding practices and access to fortified foods. The draft report was prepared by Frongillo EA et al. in 2003 for the Pan American Health Organization. 13. In Colombia, Tharrey M et al. adapted new food-based complementary feeding recommendations using linear programming. The findings were published in the Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition in December 2017 (Volume 65, Issue 6, Pages 667-672). 14. Ecuador's National Health and Nutrition Survey (ENSANUT-ECU) 2011-2013 provided harmonized data for the Global Dietary Database. The survey was conducted by the Ministry of Public Health and the National Institute of Statistics and Census in Quito, Ecuador. 15. Guatemala's Optifood study, supported by Frances Knight, analyzed nutritional gaps among children aged 6-23 months and their mothers. The final report, titled Brechas Nutricionales, was published in 2016 by INCAP. 16. The Mexican National Health and Nutrition Survey 2012 provided harmonized data for the Global Dietary Database. The survey was conducted by the National Institute of Public Health in Mexico. 17. In Peru, unpublished dietary intake data from infants and young children participating in the Sembrando la Dieta Andina project were analyzed. The baseline survey was conducted in 2015 by the Instituto de Investigación Nutricional (IIN) and Grupo Yanapai. 18. The Bangladesh Integrated Household Survey (BIHS) 2011-2012 provided harmonized data for the Global Dietary Database. The survey was conducted by the International Food Policy Research Institute. 19. In Cambodia, the ARCH Project Phase 1 analyzed child feeding practices. Alissa Pries and Helen Keller International provided the processed data. 20. In China, Wu Q et al. conducted a study to improve the intake of nutritious food among children aged 6-23 months in Wuyi County. The findings were published in the Croatian Medical Journal in April 2013 (Volume 54, Issue 2, Pages 157-170). 21. The Indian National Institute of Nutrition provided data on rural dietary and nutritional status from 2009-2012. The dataset was harmonized for the Global Dietary Database. 22. In Indonesia, the ARCH Project Phase 2 analyzed child feeding practices. Alissa Pries and Helen Keller International provided the processed data. 23. The SMILING Project in Indonesia, led by Fahmida U et al., explored food-based approaches to ensure dietary adequacy. The findings were published in Maternal & Child Health Journal in January 2019 (Volume 23, Supplement 1, Pages 55-66). 24. Israel's Mabat Infant National Health and Nutrition Survey (2009-2012) provided data on child nutrition. The survey was conducted by the Israel Center for Disease Control. 25. The Seventh Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KNHANES VII-2) 2017 provided harmonized data for the Global Dietary Database. 26. The SMILING Project in Lao PDR analyzed dietary adequacy for women and children. The findings were reported in 2019. 27. In Nepal, the ARCH Project Phases 1 and 2 analyzed child feeding practices. Alissa Pries and Helen Keller International provided the processed data.
